title: 08. Microservices & Architecture Patterns: Bulkhead Pattern

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** The bulkhead pattern isolates failures by partitioning a service's resources (thread pools, connection pools, semaphores) per downstream dependency or per tenant, so that a slow or failing dependency cannot exhaust the resources needed to serve other dependencies — preventing a single point of failure from cascading into a system-wide outage.

The name comes from ship design. A large ship's hull is divided into watertight compartments called bulkheads, separated by sealed doors. If the hull is breached below the waterline in one compartment, only that compartment floods; the bulkheads contain the damage and the ship stays afloat. Without bulkheads, a single breach would flood the entire hull and sink the ship. The same principle applies to software: if a service's threads, connections, or memory are shared across all work, a single slow downstream can fill the shared pool and sink the entire service. The bulkhead pattern partitions those resources so a failure in one partition cannot consume the resources of another. The idea was popularized for software by Netflix around 2011–2012 as part of Hystrix: every remote dependency got its own thread pool, so a slow metadata service could fill only the metadata pool, leaving the recommendation service's other pools free to call user-preference, image, and catalog services. When the metadata service went slow, only the metadata pool filled; the recommendation service degraded (no personalization) but stayed responsive, and the rest of the site kept working.

The most common bulkhead implementation is a thread pool per downstream dependency. A service has, say, four downstreams (user, catalog, inventory, payment) and assigns each a pool of 20 threads. Calls to each downstream execute only on that downstream's pool. If the inventory service goes slow, its pool fills — the 20 threads are all blocked on slow inventory calls — but the other 60 threads (for user, catalog, payment) keep working. The caller sees degraded behavior for inventory (calls queue and eventually time out or are rejected), but its calls to user, catalog, and payment continue at full speed. The bulkhead has contained the blast radius. Compare this to a shared pool of 80 threads: 80 slow inventory calls would fill the entire pool, and calls to user, catalog, and payment would queue behind them and time out — the entire service would be down, even though three of its four dependencies were healthy. The shared-pool failure mode is the classic cascading failure that took down Netflix in 2011 and many other services since.

The second common implementation is a semaphore (counting permit) bulkhead, which is lighter weight because it does not require dedicated threads. Instead of allocating threads, the bulkhead limits the number of concurrent calls to a downstream: when the limit is reached, additional calls are rejected immediately (or queued, depending on the policy). This works well when the calling code is already asynchronous or reactive (so a thread is not blocked per call), and it scales to many downstreams without the thread overhead. Resilience4j, the modern Java successor to Hystrix, supports both thread-pool and semaphore bulkheads. The trade-off: thread-pool bulkheads are stronger isolation (a blocked thread is truly separate, and the pool can be sized for the downstream's latency profile) but more expensive (each thread is ~1 MB of stack); semaphore bulkheads are cheaper but provide only concurrency limiting, not true thread isolation — a slow call still blocks its thread, even though the semaphore limits how many calls can be in flight at once. For modern reactive or async code, semaphore bulkheads are usually sufficient; for blocking code (servlets, JDBC), thread-pool bulkheads are the safer choice.

The deeper design lesson is that bulkheading is about explicit resource budgeting. Without bulkheads, a service implicitly assumes that all downstreams are equally fast and equally reliable, and that the service's total capacity is the sum of its threads. With bulkheads, the architect explicitly allocates capacity per downstream: 20 threads for inventory (because it is slow but not critical), 10 for payment (critical and fast, kept small to limit the service's exposure if payment goes down), 40 for the read-heavy catalog (high concurrency, fast). These budgets are tuned to each downstream's latency profile and importance, and they are reviewed as the system evolves. The bulkhead also makes capacity planning visible: if the inventory pool is consistently full (rejections are frequent), the team knows either to grow the pool or to make inventory calls faster. This visibility is a side benefit that often surprises teams adopting bulkheads — they discover downstreams they thought were fast were actually slow, and downstreams they thought were critical were actually tolerant of rejection. The bulkhead is both a resilience pattern and an observability tool: it makes the service's dependency profile explicit and measurable.

The pattern's trade-offs are real. Bulkheading introduces resource overhead (N downstreams × pool size threads, each with stack memory), configuration complexity (each pool must be sized, monitored, and tuned), and a new failure mode (pool exhaustion causes rejections, which the caller must handle gracefully — typically by a fallback or a fast-fail). The alternative — a shared pool — is simpler but risks cascading failure. For most production microservices, the bulkhead's protection is worth the overhead, especially for services with many downstreams or with downstreams of varying reliability. The pattern composes well with circuit breakers: the bulkhead limits the blast radius of a slow downstream to its own pool, and the breaker eventually trips and stops sending traffic to that downstream, freeing the pool. Netflix's Hystrix bundled both, and modern systems using Resilience4j, Envoy, or Istio follow the same composition.

### ASCII Diagram
```

       +-----------+        +---------------------------------+
       |  client   | -----> |  80 shared threads              |
       +-----------+        |   |   |   |   |   |   |   | ... |

                            | slow (5s)|  | fast    |  | fast    |
                            +---------+  +---------+  +---------+
                                  ^        (queued behind slow
                                   \       inventory calls -> time out)
                                    \      --> ENTIRE SERVICE DOWN

                     bulkhead (thread pool per downstream)

       +-----------+        +----------+ +----------+ +----------+ +----------+
       |  client   | -----> | pool:    | | pool:    | | pool:    | | pool:    |
       +-----------+        | inv 20   | | usr 10   | | cat 40   | | pay 10   |
                            +----+-----+ +----+-----+ +----+-----+ +----+-----+
                                 |            |            |            |
                                 v            v            v            v
                            +---------+  +---------+  +---------+  +---------+
                            | inv slow|  | user OK |  | cat OK  |  | pay OK  |
                            +---------+  +---------+  +---------+  +---------+
                            only 20 threads block (pool fills, rejections start)
                            --> inventory degraded, user/catalog/payment UNAFFECTED
```

### Walkthrough
1. The calling service has multiple downstream dependencies. In the shared-pool model, all calls execute on the same thread pool; if one downstream (inventory) becomes slow, its calls hold threads for seconds, and within seconds the entire pool is blocked, so calls to user, catalog, and payment — even though those downstreams are healthy — queue behind the blocked threads and time out, taking the whole service down.
2. The bulkhead assigns each downstream its own thread pool (or semaphore, or connection pool), sized to that downstream's expected concurrency and latency profile. Inventory gets 20 threads (slow, low concurrency), catalog gets 40 (fast, high concurrency), payment gets 10 (fast, critical). Each downstream's calls execute only on its pool.
3. When inventory goes slow, only the inventory pool's 20 threads fill; calls beyond the pool size are rejected immediately (the caller gets a fallback or a fast-fail), and the other pools keep serving at full speed. The service degrades gracefully — inventory calls fail, but the rest of the service stays responsive — and a circuit breaker on the inventory call eventually trips, stopping traffic and freeing the pool.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Bulkhead pattern: one thread pool per downstream dependency.
# Demonstrates that a slow downstream fills only its own pool,
# leaving other downstreams' pools free to keep serving.

import time, threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ThreadPoolExecutor as TPE

class Bulkhead:
    """A bounded thread pool that rejects work when full."""
    def __init__(self, name, max_concurrent):
        self.name = name
        self.pool = TPE(max_workers=max_concurrent)
        self.sem = threading.Semaphore(max_concurrent)
        self.rejected = 0

    def submit(self, fn, *args):
        # Non-blocking acquire: if no permit, reject fast (do not queue).
        if not self.sem.acquire(blocking=False):
            self.rejected += 1
            return lambda: f"[{self.name}] REJECTED (pool full)"
        def wrapper():
            try:
                return fn(*args)
            finally:
                self.sem.release()
        return self.pool.submit(wrapper).result

# Mock downstreams. inventory is slow (2s), the others are fast (50ms).
def call_inventory():  time.sleep(2.0); return "inventory OK"
def call_user():       time.sleep(0.05); return "user OK"
def call_catalog():    time.sleep(0.05); return "catalog OK"

# One bulkhead per downstream, sized to its expected latency profile.
inv_bulk  = Bulkhead("inventory", max_concurrent=5)
usr_bulk  = Bulkhead("user",      max_concurrent=5)
cat_bulk  = Bulkhead("catalog",   max_concurrent=5)

# Simulate a burst: 10 inventory calls + 10 user calls + 10 catalog calls.
# Inventory fills its pool of 5 -> 5 rejected. User/catalog never affected.
def burst():
    results = {"inventory": [], "user": [], "catalog": []}
    for _ in range(10):
        results["inventory"].append(inv_bulk.submit(call_inventory))
        results["user"].append(usr_bulk.submit(call_user))
        results["catalog"].append(cat_bulk.submit(call_catalog))
    # Drain results (inventory futures block until 2s calls complete).
    for k in results:
        results[k] = [r() if callable(r) else r.result() for r in results[k]]
    return results

t0 = time.time()
out = burst()
print(f"elapsed: {time.time()-t0:.2f}s")
print(f"inventory accepted/rejected: "
      f"{sum(1 for r in out['inventory'] if 'OK' in r)}/"
      f"{inv_bulk.rejected}")
print(f"user      accepted/rejected: "
      f"{sum(1 for r in out['user'] if 'OK' in r)}/"
      f"{usr_bulk.rejected}")
print(f"catalog   accepted/rejected: "
      f"{sum(1 for r in out['catalog'] if 'OK' in r)}/"
      f"{cat_bulk.rejected}")
```

quiz.question: How does a thread-pool bulkhead differ from a semaphore bulkhead?
options: The team's math is correct (1000 threads across replicas) but the reasoning misses three things.
600 threads is too many for a 1 GB container — each JVM thread is ~1 MB stack, and 600 MB of stack plus heap plus off-heap leaves no room for the application.
Sizing is driven by the downstream's latency profile and the caller's expected concurrency.
A thread-pool bulkhead allocates a dedicated set of threads per downstream; calls to that downstream execute only on those threads, so a slow call blocks one of those…
quiz.explanation: A thread-pool bulkhead allocates a dedicated set of threads per downstream; calls to that downstream execute only on those threads, so a slow call blocks one of those threads but no thread from other pools.

quiz.explanation: The trade-offs are resource overhead, configuration complexity, and a new failure mode. Overhead: N downstreams × pool size threads, each with ~1 MB stack — for a service with 20 downstreams and 20-thread pools, that is 400 threads = 400 MB just for stacks, plus context-switching cost. Semaphore bulkheads reduce this but provide weaker isolation.

quiz.question: How do you size a bulkhead pool, and what signals tell you it is mis-sized?
options: Circuit breakers and bulkheads solve different problems, and breakers alone leave a critical gap.
600 threads is too many for a 1 GB container — each JVM thread is ~1 MB stack, and 600 MB of stack plus heap plus off-heap leaves no room for the application.
Beyond downstream isolation, bulkheading is used for tenant isolation: in a multi-tenant SaaS, each tenant (or tenant tier) gets its own pool of resources (threads,…
Sizing is driven by the downstream's latency profile and the caller's expected concurrency.
quiz.explanation: Sizing is driven by the downstream's latency profile and the caller's expected concurrency. The rule of thumb is pool_size = max_concurrent_calls = target_throughput * p99_latency. If the caller expects 1000 req/s to inventory and inventory's p99 latency is 50 ms, then pool_size = 1000 * 0.05 = 50 threads to handle the concurrency without queuing.
